# Perpetual → Subscription: A Transition Plan

*(Illustrative model: ~$400M revenue — $180M license/upgrade, $160M maintenance, $60M services; ~5,000 customers. Replace with your actuals; the ratios and mechanics are what transfer.)*

---

## 1. The strategic verdict and five design principles

The competitor didn't lose 20% of its base because it moved to subscription. It lost them because it **forced** migration, **shocked** prices, and **held features hostage** on a short clock. Those are all avoidable design choices.

**Principles that govern every decision below:**

1. **Never revoke what was sold.** Perpetual licenses stay perpetual, forever, in writing. The transition is won by *pull* (new value only available on subscription), not push.
2. **Make the trough deep and short, not shallow and long.** A 2-year, well-forecast dip is financeable. A 5-year ambiguous drift destroys management credibility and invites activists.
3. **Change the scoreboard before the numbers change.** Reset investor metrics one to two quarters *ahead* of the revenue decline, not in the quarter you miss.
4. **Don't ask the sales force to fund the strategy.** Reps who execute correctly must earn the same or more in the transition years. Comp is the single highest-leverage lever and the most commonly botched.
5. **No dual-track ambiguity for new business.** Perpetual comes off the new-logo price book on Day 1. Ambiguity guarantees reps sell the old thing.

**Prerequisite gate:** do not open migration to the installed base until the cloud/subscription product reaches functional parity on the top 5 workflows covering ~80% of usage, plus SSO, data residency, and an admin/entitlement console. Migrating customers onto an inferior product is exactly how you manufacture a 20% churn event. Budget 2–4 quarters of engineering ahead of the commercial launch.

---

## 2. Offer architecture: three lanes

| Lane | Who | Offer | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Cloud subscription** *(destination)* | All new logos; installed base that opts in | Annual/multi-year SaaS, ratable revenue, annual-upfront billing | The end state; where all new innovation ships |
| **B. Term license (on-prem)** *(bridge)* | Regulated, air-gapped, sovereignty-constrained, large-procurement accounts | 3-year on-prem subscription, no perpetual right | Under ASC 606 the distinct license component is recognized **upfront**, cushioning the trough — while still converting the customer to a renewable contract |
| **C. Legacy perpetual + maintenance** *(runoff)* | Existing holders only; closed to new logos immediately | Maintained, supported, security-patched. Frozen feature set as of Release N+1 | Honors the entitlement, removes the "we're being extorted" narrative |

**On Lane B:** term licenses are the most underused instrument in these transitions. They convert a customer to renewable, contracted revenue while preserving a large slug of upfront recognition. They also solve the "our biggest customers physically cannot buy cloud" problem. Report them as a separate line so analysts can see the mix; treat them as a bridge, not a destination, and sunset new term-license sales in Year 4.

**Feature fork (the engine of pull):** publish a dated roadmap showing that all new modules, AI features, integrations, and analytics ship to Lanes A and B only. Lane C receives security, compliance, and platform-compatibility updates for a **committed 5 years**, with a published end-of-support date given 36 months' notice. That's a long, honorable runway — and it is the thing that makes migration inevitable without making it coercive.

---

## 3. Migration offer for existing license holders

The core promise, in a single sentence to be used in every customer conversation:

> *"You keep the license you bought, forever. If you choose to move, we'll credit the investment you've already made and cap your costs for three years."*

**The migration ladder (decaying, to concentrate the trough):**

| Program window | Trade-in credit on original net license fee | Year-1 subscription price | Year 2 | Year 3 | Renewal cap |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Wave 1 (Q1–Q4 of Yr 1) | 25%, applied over 3 years | Maintenance-equivalent (≈ 0.55× list ACV) | 0.80× list | 1.0× list | 5%/yr, 3-yr protection |
| Wave 2 (Yr 2) | 15% | 0.70× list | 0.85× list | 1.0× list | 5%/yr, 2-yr protection |
| Wave 3 (Yr 3) | 7% | 0.85× list | 1.0× list | — | 5%/yr |
| After (Yr 4+) | 0% | List | — | — | Standard |

**Non-price sweeteners** (cheaper than discount, and they don't reset price expectations):
- Migration services and data conversion at no charge in Waves 1–2 (cost you ~$3–8K/customer; worth far more than an equivalent discount).
- Free upgrade to the next support tier for 24 months.
- One additional module free for 12 months (a planted expansion seed — measure attach at renewal).
- Named migration architect for accounts >$100K ACV.
- Executive-sponsor program for the top 100 accounts: CEO/CPO roadmap sessions, design-partner status on new features.

**The escalator on Lane C:** apply a 7% annual increase to legacy maintenance (a normal, defensible CPI-plus adjustment), while Lane A pricing is locked. Over three years this closes most of the economic gap without any coercion. Do **not** exceed ~8%/year and do **not** threaten support withdrawal — that is precisely the competitor's mistake.

**Sequencing matters:** migrate mid-market and high-engagement/cloud-ready cohorts first (fast, cheap, generates reference proof and cohort data for investors). Save the hardest enterprise and regulated accounts for Years 2–3 via Lane B. Do not lead with your ten largest, most-customized customers.

---

## 4. Pricing: balancing trough depth against adoption

**The anchor ratio.** Set list subscription ACV so that:
- **Years 1–2:** customer TCO is clearly *lower* than perpetual (the adoption incentive)
- **Year ~4:** crossover / parity
- **Year 5+:** vendor takes 1.5–1.8× the 5-year perpetual value (the payoff)

A perpetual deal of $100K license + $20K/yr maintenance yields $180K over 5 years. Price subscription at **~$40–45K ACV** (≈ 35–38% of license + first-year maintenance). Five-year subscription value = $200–225K → **1.15–1.25×**, rising to 1.5×+ with the standard 5% escalator and expansion. That's the right zone: rich enough to justify the trough, cheap enough that the customer's CFO signs.

**Discipline rules:**
- **Never discount list ACV for new logos.** All concession flows through the time-boxed migration ladder. This protects the long-run price and makes the ladder's expiry genuinely credible.
- **Annual-upfront billing is the default.** Multi-year prepay offered at ≤7%/yr discount, capped at ~15% of bookings (it front-loads cash but hollows out Year 2–3 collections).
- **Price expansion, not just conversion.** Every migration conversation is a re-scope: modules, users, environments. Target cohort ARR uplift of **1.25–1.4×** prior maintenance + amortized license spend. This uplift is the metric that convinces investors the model change creates value rather than just re-timing it.

### The trough, quantified

| | T0 | T1 | T2 | T3 | T4 | T5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Perpetual license | 180 | 100 | 45 | 15 | 5 | 0 |
| Term license (upfront portion) | 0 | 15 | 25 | 20 | 10 | 0 |
| Maintenance | 160 | 155 | 138 | 110 | 85 | 60 |
| Subscription (ratable) | 0 | 20 | 65 | 130 | 205 | 285 |
| Services | 60 | 62 | 65 | 68 | 72 | 80 |
| **GAAP revenue** | **400** | **352** | **338** | **343** | **377** | **425** |
| *vs. T0* | — | *−12%* | *−15%* | *−14%* | *−6%* | *+6%* |
| **Exit ARR** | **160** | **195** | **250** | **315** | **395** | **480** |
| Subscription mix | 0% | 10% | 27% | 44% | 61% | 74% |
| FCF margin | 20% | 13% | 8% | 11% | 17% | 23% |

**The headline you commit to:** *revenue troughs at ~−15% in T2, returns to prior peak in T5, while ARR compounds at ~25% every single year of the transition and gross margin expands 400–600bps by T5.* ARR never declines — that is the load-bearing fact of the entire investor story.

**Funding the trough:** (a) redeploy perpetual-era spend — upgrade-release engineering, packaging/distribution, license-audit function — roughly 3–5 pts of opex; (b) hold headcount flat outside cloud engineering and customer success in T1–T2; (c) put a revolver in place *before* you need it; (d) consider a modest buyback authorization as a confidence signal rather than a large one that constrains flexibility.

---

## 5. Sales compensation redesign

**The governing rule:** a rep who does exactly what the new strategy wants earns *at least* what they earned last year. Anything else and you lose your best people in the first two quarters — which is the actual mechanism behind most "failed" transitions.

**Design:**

| Element | Mechanic |
|---|---|
| **Credit basis** | Pay on **ACV × a transition multiplier**: 3.0× in T1, 2.5× in T2, 2.0× in T3, 1.0× (pure ACV) from T4. Publish the full 3-year schedule on Day 1 so reps can plan. |
| **Payout timing** | Full first-year commission paid at booking (on signature + first invoice), not as revenue is recognized. Protects rep cash flow, which is what they actually care about. |
| **Bridge pay** | 6-quarter guarantee at 75% of trailing-12-month earnings for reps who hit conversion-activity targets. Costs ~2–3% of subscription revenue in T1–T2. Cheap insurance. |
| **Perpetual** | Removed from new-logo price book Day 1. Legacy true-ups carry 0.4× credit and require SVP approval. |
| **Migration motion** | Split it out: a dedicated **Install Base / Customer Success** team on quota of *converted ARR + conversion count*, with a per-account SPIFF ($1–3K) in Waves 1–2. Frees quota-carriers for new logos and expansion. |
| **Retention gate** | 25% of commission on new subscription deals held back and released at first renewal; full clawback on first-year churn or downgrade >20%. |
| **Multi-year** | Modest kicker (1.15× credit) for 3-year terms with annual billing; no kicker for deep prepay discounts. |
| **Leadership** | Same logic up the chain — regional VP variable tied to net-new ARR, conversion rate against installed-base plan, and NRR. |

**Also change the hiring profile.** Perpetual reps are trained to hunt large, episodic, discount-heavy deals; subscription requires land-and-expand and value realization. Expect and plan for **15–25% voluntary attrition** in the first four quarters. Over-hire by that amount in T1 rather than scrambling in T2, and stand up an enablement program on ROI-based selling and migration-objection handling before the plan launches.
